chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Building Blocks of a DCF

lessons.title: Estimating Cost of Equity for Indian Stocks: Risk-Free Rate, Beta and Equity Risk Premium

children.text: Of the three inputs behind every valuation, risk is the one you cannot look up. Cash flows are reported in annual reports. Growth shows up in ten years of history on screener.in. But no filing tells you what return shareholders require from a stock. You have to estimate it, and a two percentage point error in the cost of equity can move a DCF value by 20% or more. This lesson gives you a disciplined way to build the number for Indian stocks, and the judgement to sanity-check it.

body.text: The cost of equity is the return you need to be paid to own this stock instead of a Government of India bond. CAPM gives you a disciplined starting point for that number. It does not give you the answer.

children.text: The Framework: CAPM
The
Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM)
breaks the cost of equity into three pieces you can reason about separately.

markDefs.definition: A model that estimates the return investors require from a stock as the risk-free rate plus the stock's beta multiplied by the equity risk premium.

body.caption: Cost of equity = risk-free rate + beta × equity risk premium

children.text: Risk-free rate (Rf):
what you earn for waiting, with no business risk.
Equity risk premium (ERP):
the extra return investors demand for holding the stock market as a whole instead of government bonds.
Beta (β):
how much of the market's risk this particular stock carries.

body.title: Cost of equity for a beta-1.0 Indian stock: 13.5% (illustrative)

children.text: Piece 1: The Risk-Free Rate
For a DCF in rupees, use the yield on the
10-year Government of India bond
. Three rules keep it consistent:

markDefs.definition: The benchmark long-term government security (G-sec) issued by the Government of India and auctioned by the RBI. Its yield is the standard long-term risk-free rate for rupee valuations.

children.text: Match the currency.
Your cash flows are in rupees, which carry Indian inflation. The US 10-year Treasury yield, typically several percentage points lower, would badly overstate value.
Match the horizon.
A business lasts decades, so use a long-dated bond, not the RBI repo rate, a 91-day T-bill or a bank FD rate.
Use today's yield.
Value on the date you are valuing. If you believe current yields are unusually high or low, some analysts use a normalised rate, but state it explicitly.

body.label: Recent range of India's 10-year G-sec yield
body.context: Over roughly the first half of the 2020s. Always check the current yield on the date of your valuation. This lesson uses 6.5% for illustration.

body.label: Reserve Bank of India
body.description: The RBI publishes government securities auction results and market data, including benchmark 10-year G-sec yields. Financial newspapers and broker platforms also quote the benchmark yield daily.

body.title: Advanced: is the Indian G-sec really risk-free?

children.text: A rupee-denominated Government of India bond is about as close to risk-free as a rupee investor can get, because the government borrows in its own currency. Some global practitioners, notably in the approach popularised by Professor Aswath Damodaran, still subtract a default spread from the G-sec yield because India's sovereign credit rating sits at the lower end of investment grade. They then add a matching country risk premium to the equity risk premium instead.

For most Indian investors valuing Indian companies in rupees, using the G-sec yield directly with an India-level equity risk premium gives a very similar cost of equity. What matters is consistency: do not use a reduced risk-free rate and a mature-market ERP together, or the country risk disappears from your valuation entirely.
Piece 2: The Equity Risk Premium for India
The
equity risk premium (ERP)
is the most debated number in finance, because it is an expectation about the future. There are two broad ways to estimate it.

markDefs.definition: The additional annual return investors expect from the broad equity market over the risk-free rate, as compensation for equity risk.

body.title: Two ways to estimate India's ERP

columns.label: Historical premium
points: Method: long-run Sensex or Nifty return minus G-sec return
Evidence: the Sensex has compounded at roughly 15% a year in price terms since its 1978-79 base
Strength: based on what actually happened
Weakness: very sensitive to start and end dates, and India's high inflation eras distort it

columns.label: Forward-looking premium
points: Method: a mature-market ERP plus a country risk premium for India, or an ERP implied from current index prices and expected earnings
Evidence: widely cited practitioner estimates for India have tended to sit in roughly the 6% to 8% range
Weakness: depends on the model and its own assumptions

body.text: This lesson uses an ERP of 7.0%. Pick one well-reasoned ERP and use it consistently across every company you value. Changing the ERP stock by stock is a way to reach the answer you wanted, not an estimate of risk. Company-specific risk belongs in beta, in your cash flow scenarios, or in an explicit and clearly labelled adjustment.

children.text: Piece 3: Beta
Beta

measures how sensitive a stock is to the market. A beta of 1.4 means that when the Nifty has moved 1%, the stock has tended to move about 1.4% in the same direction. CAPM assumes that only this market-related risk earns a premium, because company-specific risks can be diversified away in a portfolio.

markDefs.definition: A measure of how much a stock's returns have moved with the market's returns. A beta of 1 moves in line with the market; above 1 amplifies market moves; below 1 dampens them.

children.text: Regression beta: what websites show

The beta you see on Indian stock data platforms is usually a regression beta: the slope of the stock's weekly or monthly returns plotted against an index such as the Nifty 50, over two to five years. It is quick, but noisy.

body.caption: Why a single stock's regression beta can mislead

cells: The stock does not trade on many days, so its returns look disconnected from the index and beta comes out artificially low
A demerger, a big acquisition or a governance scare in the sample period distorts the slope
Any stock with a major corporate action
The past business mix or leverage no longer matches today's company
Companies after large capex or deleveraging
Estimates for a single stock often have wide error ranges, so a beta of 0.9 could plausibly be 0.6 or 1.2
Beta against the Nifty 50 can differ from beta against the Nifty 500

children.text: Bottom-up beta: the better approach
Instead of trusting one noisy number, take betas for a group of comparable listed companies, strip out the effect of each company's debt to get an
unlevered beta
, average those, then add back your company's own debt level.

markDefs.definition: The beta a company would have with no debt. It reflects business risk only. Also called asset beta.

body.caption: Unlever each peer, then relever at your company's own debt-to-equity ratio (market values)

children.text: Worked Example: Cost of Equity for Kaveri Ridge Cement

In the last lesson we simply assumed Kaveri Ridge Cement's shareholders require 12%. Now estimate it. Four listed cement peers have the following regression betas and market-value debt-to-equity ratios. The tax rate is 25%.
Round the average unlevered beta to 0.75. Kaveri Ridge has net debt of ₹1,500 crore and an equity market value of about ₹7,643 crore, a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.20.

The estimate of about 12.5% is close to the 12% assumed earlier, but it is now built from observable inputs. If Kaveri Ridge doubled its debt, its relevered beta and cost of equity would rise, even though the cement business itself had not become any riskier.
How Beta Changes the Answer
Hold the risk-free rate at 6.5% and the ERP at 7.0%, and look at three fictional Indian companies with different betas.

body.title: Cost of equity by beta (Rf 6.5%, ERP 7.0%, illustrative)

children.text: Now see why this matters. For a business whose cash flows grow at 5% a year forever, value equals next year's cash flow multiplied by 1 ÷ (Ke - g).

body.text: Many Indian valuation reports add a "company-specific risk premium" of 2% to 5% for small or unlisted companies. Sometimes that is justified. Often it is double counting: the same risks are already in a higher beta, in cautious cash flow forecasts, or both. Whenever you see an extra premium, ask exactly which risk it covers that is not already captured elsewhere.

children.text: Sanity Checks Before You Use the Number

body.title: Five checks on any cost of equity
steps: Is it above the company's own pre-tax cost of borrowing? Shareholders are paid after lenders, so they must require more.
Is a beta-1.0 stock getting a cost of equity broadly in line with long-run Indian equity market returns, in the low-to-mid teens?
Did a small cap come out with a very low beta? Check its trading volumes before trusting it.
Are the risk-free rate, ERP and cash flows all in rupees and all consistent in how they treat country risk?
Does the answer rank sensibly against peers? A leveraged metals company should not have a lower cost of equity than an FMCG leader.

body.title: Calculate a regression beta yourself in Excel
steps: Download two years of daily closing prices for the stock and for the Nifty 50 from the historical data section of the NSE website.
Convert both to weekly closing prices, using the same trading day each week.
Calculate weekly returns for each: (this week's close ÷ last week's close) - 1.
In an empty cell, enter =SLOPE(stock returns range, Nifty returns range). The result is the regression beta.
Repeat for three or four peers, unlever each, and compare the average with the single-stock figure.

children.text: Check Your Understanding

body.title: Calculate the cost of equity
body.prompt: The 10-year G-sec yield is 6.8%, your ERP for India is 7.0% and a private bank's beta is 1.2. What is its cost of equity using CAPM, in %?

body.title: Relever a beta
body.prompt: The average unlevered beta for listed hospital chains is 0.90. The hospital company you are valuing has a market-value debt-to-equity ratio of 0.50 and a tax rate of 25%. What is its relevered beta? Answer to two decimal places.
body.explanation: Levered beta = 0.90 × [1 + (1 - 0.25) × 0.50] = 0.90 × 1.375 = 1.24. More debt means shareholders bear more of the same business risk.

body.title: Choose the risk-free rate
body.question: You are building a rupee DCF for an Indian IT services company that earns most of its revenue in US dollars. Which risk-free rate should you use?
options: The US 10-year Treasury yield, because revenue is in dollars
The 10-year Government of India bond yield
The one-year SBI fixed deposit rate
body.explanation: The rate must match the currency of the cash flows in your model. If you project cash flows in rupees, which carry Indian inflation expectations, use the rupee 10-year G-sec yield. The repo rate and FD rates are short-term. You would use the US Treasury yield only if you built the whole model in dollars, with dollar cash flows and a dollar ERP.

body.title: Beta without debt
body.textWithBlank: A beta with the effect of debt removed, reflecting only business risk, is called an ___ beta.
body.explanation: Unlevered, or asset, beta isolates business risk. You average unlevered betas across peers, then relever at your company's own debt-to-equity ratio.

body.title: The suspiciously cheap small cap
body.scenario: Vikram, a Hyderabad-based investor, finds a small-cap auto components maker whose stock trades on only a few days each week on BSE. A data platform shows its beta as 0.40. Using a 6.5% risk-free rate and 7.0% ERP, he calculates a cost of equity of 9.3%. His DCF then shows the stock is worth nearly double its current price. Listed auto component peers with good liquidity have betas between 1.0 and 1.3.
body.prompt: What is wrong with Vikram's cost of equity, and how should he fix it?
body.modelAnswer:
1. The beta is almost certainly distorted by illiquidity. A stock that does not trade most days shows returns that appear unrelated to the Nifty, which pushes the regression slope towards zero. It does not mean the business is safe.
2. A cost of equity of 9.3% is a red flag on its own. It is barely above the risk-free rate and probably below what the company pays its bank for loans. Shareholders in a small, illiquid, cyclical business cannot sensibly require less than lenders.
3. The business is cyclical. Auto components demand rises and falls with vehicle sales, which should mean a beta at or above 1, as the liquid peers show.
4. The fix: use a bottom-up beta. Unlever the liquid peers' betas, average them, and relever at this company's own debt-to-equity ratio. With a relevered beta of around 1.2, the cost of equity would be about 14.9%.
5. The consequence: moving from 9.3% to around 14.9% will cut the DCF value sharply, and the "nearly double" upside is likely to disappear. The apparent bargain came from the discount rate, not the business.

points: CAPM estimates the cost of equity as the risk-free rate plus beta multiplied by the equity risk premium.
For rupee cash flows, use the current 10-year Government of India bond yield as the risk-free rate.
India's equity risk premium is an estimate. Choose one well-reasoned figure and apply it consistently across companies.
Single-stock regression betas are noisy and can be badly distorted by illiquidity. Prefer a bottom-up beta from unlevered peer betas.
Relever beta at your company's own market-value debt-to-equity ratio: more debt means a higher cost of equity.
Sanity-check the result: the cost of equity must exceed the company's cost of debt and rank sensibly against peers.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Kaveri Ridge Cement Ltd, the peer companies and the individuals named are fictional, and all betas and ratios are illustrative. Yield, index return and equity risk premium ranges are approximate and change over time. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before making investment decisions.
